Series::dist¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::dist(const Series& other) const
Series Series::dist(const Series& other, double p) const

What It Does¶

Returns a single number: the p-norm of the difference self - other.

It is the norm-based notion of “how far apart are these two tensors”. The two inputs are subtracted elementwise, the whole difference is treated as one flat bag of values, and its p-norm is taken. The result is always a 0-D scalar, no matter the shape of the inputs.

Different p give different notions of distance:

  • p = 2 (the default) — ordinary Euclidean / straight-line distance: sqrt(sum((a - b)^2)). For a 2-D input this is the Frobenius distance.

  • p = 1 — Manhattan / taxicab distance: sum(|a - b|).

  • p = inf — Chebyshev distance: max(|a - b|), the single largest coordinate gap.

  • general p — (sum(|a - b|^p))^(1/p).

The one-argument form dist(other) is exactly dist(other, 2.0).

The difference is a normal broadcast subtraction, so self and other do not have to be the same shape as long as they broadcast together.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&): the tensor to measure the distance to. Must broadcast against self.

p (double, default 2.0): which norm of the difference to take. 1, 2, any positive real, or inf (std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity()).

Returns¶

Series A 0-D scalar — the p-norm of self - other. Real dtype; integer inputs are promoted.

Gradient¶

Differentiable in both operands. For p = 2, d/da dist(a, b) = (a - b) / dist(a, b) — the unit vector pointing from b to a. It is undefined when a == b (the 0/0 at the cone tip); a reverse pass there produces nan/0 rather than raising, the same as norm.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default is the Euclidean distance, handed back as a scalar.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 6.0, 3.0});
std::cout << a.dist(b);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=5

The difference is [-3, -4, 0]; sqrt(9 + 16 + 0) = 5.

Example 2. The p argument selects the norm.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 6.0, 3.0});
std::cout << "p=1  : " << a.dist(b, 1.0);
std::cout << "p=2  : " << a.dist(b, 2.0);
std::cout << "p=3  : " << a.dist(b, 3.0);
std::cout << "p=inf: " << a.dist(b, std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity());

Output¶

p=1  : pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=7p=2  : pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=5p=3  : pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4.4979414p=inf: pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4

p = 1 sums the gaps (3 + 4 + 0 = 7); p = inf takes the largest (4); p = 3 sits between p = 2 and p = inf, always closer to the max as p grows.

Example 3. A 2-D input is flattened first — this is the Frobenius distance.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 8.0}});
std::cout << a.dist(b);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4

Only one entry differs, by 4, so every p-norm of the difference is 4. Shape plays no role beyond defining which entries line up.

Example 4. The distance from a tensor to itself is 0.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
std::cout << a.dist(a);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0

This is also the point where the p = 2 gradient is undefined — see the Gradient section.

Example 5. dist is sub followed by norm: a.dist(b, p) equals (a - b).norm(p).

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 6.0, 3.0});
std::cout << "a.dist(b, 3) = " << a.dist(b, 3.0);
std::cout << "(a-b).norm(3) = " << a.sub(b).norm(3.0);

Output¶

a.dist(b, 3) = pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=4.4979414(a-b).norm(3) = pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[4.4979414]

Same value. dist always normalizes the result to a 0-D scalar; norm with a non-standard p can hand back a [1] vector, which is the one shape difference to be aware of.

Example 6. The difference broadcasts, so the two operands need not match shape.

auto a = pluss::make_series({3.0, 4.0, 12.0});
std::cout << a.dist(pluss::make_series(0.0));

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=13

a - 0 is just a; sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = 13. This is the length of a itself — x.dist(zeros_like(x)) is x.norm().

Example 7. Gradient: for p = 2 it is the unit vector from b toward a.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 6.0, 3.0});
a.dist(b).reverse();
std::cout << a.sensitivity();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.6, -0.8, 0]

(a - b) / dist(a, b) = [-3, -4, 0] / 5. The vector has length 1.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The result is always a 0-D scalar, even for p values where a bare norm(p) would return a [1] vector.

  • The two operands are combined with a broadcast subtraction, not a distance-matrix construction. For all pairwise distances between the rows of two matrices, reach for stat’s cdist instead.

  • p must be positive. p = 0 is not a norm and is rejected.

  • The p = 2 gradient is undefined at a == b. If your objective can drive the two together, add an epsilon or guard the step.

  • dist promotes to a real dtype; the answer is never integral.

Summary¶

dist(other, p = 2) is the p-norm of self - other, as a scalar:

  • p = 2 Euclidean (default), p = 1 Manhattan, p = inf Chebyshev

  • inputs broadcast; the difference is flattened before the norm

  • always a 0-D scalar result

  • differentiable; the p = 2 gradient is the unit vector between the operands, undefined where they coincide

See Also¶

  • Series::norm: the p-norm of a single tensor — dist is (a - b).norm(p) pinned to a scalar.

  • Series::sub: the elementwise difference dist measures.

  • Series::renorm: the other norm-constraint op — rescale sub-tensors so their norm stays under a cap.
